notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg2200.tlg00542.opp-gr: In §3 ἀπὸ τοῦ τάφου seems to lack a verb (perhaps 'dragging [me] from the tomb'); rendered loosely. In §11 'S rfj' is a garbled scan, evidently ὦ Γῆ ('O Earth'). The opening of §11 (μετὰ τούτων) read as 'with them [freedom and laws]'.

15.1: the Greek is compressed: 'I persuaded [the tyrant], by what I showed him, no longer to seek what no longer existed'. 18.1: the imperative 'pity' is singular in the Greek. 20.1: 'ἐπέδωκα ὦκα' is a dittography; I read ἐπέδωκα. 22: I have taken the sentence as a question ('must I answer this, when...?'), and its syntax is awkward. 24.1: 'μηκέτ᾿ ἐχαρισάμην' looks corrupt; I translated on a supposed 'ὃ μηκέτ᾿ ἔστιν' ('[him who] is no more'), so the reading is uncertain. 25.1: the text is broken after 'ἐπαίδευσεν'; the fragment 'σαμένῃ' (a feminine participle, perhaps '[to the city] that had ...') cannot be translated. The edition's 'ἠγόρευθα' and 'ἀπεύχερθαι' are read as ἠγόρευσα and ἀπεύχεσθαι. 29: 'ἔνα' is read as ἵνα.

32: ἀκούει read as ἀκούειν. 43: ἴδει read as ἔδει. 45: κατ’ ἔχειν read as κατέχειν. 46: 'τοῖς λειν ὑμᾶς βουλομένοις' is corrupt; something like κακῶς λέγειν or διαβάλλειν ('slander') is presumably lost, and 'slander' is conjectural. 46: 'by me' renders the sense implied by the context (cf. the following line); the text has only 'about my own'.
In 47.1 οἶσον is taken as the neuter future participle of φέρω, agreeing with ψήφισμα. In 47.1 the 'they' of 'what wrong have they suffered' refers to the people.

nodes.text: XLII.

A tyrant demanded a handsome youth from a neighbouring city, threatening war if he did not get him. The city accepted the war. The tyrant attacked. While the city was under siege, the father killed the youth and threw him from the wall. When the tyrant had withdrawn, [the father] is tried for murder.
The declamation.

This too, gentlemen, might be part of my misfortune: that some are trying to persuade you that they have been, and are, better disposed towards my son than I am. If they were urging you to kill me as the most wretched of all men, I would consider those who did this both good and humane, and my benefactors; for to those who must live in the greatest grief, death is no small gain. But since they are trying to do this by means of an accusation and a vote, and with charges such as you have heard, I hold that it is not ceasing to exist, but dying on such grounds, that is most terrible, and so I think I must make a defence before you of what I did not shrink from doing.

And you too, gentlemen, ought to help those who are in as bad a state as I am, rather than those who, with fortune on their side, attack men who choose and do everything on behalf of you and of the whole city. For it would make no sense that the man who has surpassed all in goodwill towards you should die as the basest of men towards his own family.

What was just, then, was that I should now be allowed to sit by the tomb and not leave, by night or by day, the place that has received my dearest child. For the rest of you it is the time to spend in temples, sacrifices and hymns, since you expected the most terrible things but suffered none of what you had reason to fear; but for me, who have lost <my son>, [it is the time] to weep for him, to honour him, and to listen to those who console me, to whom I know I owe great thanks. But since certain men have appeared, [drawing me] away from the tomb and putting on trial a man who cannot even stand upright, and through me are slandering the community, if it is thought to raise citizens who dare such deeds not from love of the city but from hatred of their own, I beg you all not to allow a worse reputation to fall either on the city or on me, but to show yourselves to me today such judges as you would have thought it right to obtain, if you had planned the same as I, succeeded in the same way, and were on trial on the same grounds.

4. I had resolved, gentlemen, never to remind you of what I have suffered for your sake; for the patriot, I think, must everywhere put the common good before himself, and when he has been of service and has done a good deed, he must keep silent about it himself and blush when another speaks of it. But since these men force me to say what I would least have wished, for my whole defence lies in these things, gentlemen, consider these words to belong not to the speaker but to those who do not allow them to be passed over in silence; men who not only wrong both me and you, but also take away no small part of the tyrant's grief by putting on trial and harassing the man whom he considers the most hateful of all to himself.

But these men perhaps must serve him in everything; you, however, who owe him no favour and have also sworn an oath, must act not in ways that would please that god-hated man, but rather in ways that will pain him. And this would happen if, even before my defence, you were to say to yourselves what it would be natural <for me to say>.

6. I married a wife, gentlemen, according to the laws of the city, and, unhappy man, I prayed that from this marriage children would be born to me as helpers to me and to the city, speaking, proposing measures, serving in war, gladly accepting death for the land that bore them. And I asked that they be good and, above all, self-controlled.

And the <gods> gave, as they ought not to have done, this very boy whom you praise, splendid in appearance, excellent in character, the same boy who by his beauty drew all eyes to himself and by his self-control surpassed his beauty. Anyone naming him would add 'the handsome'; and I, ill-starred man, rejoiced to hear it and thought I ought to be grateful to the gods for this too. But I was, it seems, destined to be ruined by this fine gift.

I raised him, then, as was fitting for such a boy, with every precaution keeping away every plot. He had no need of guarding by overseers, yet attendants followed him, so that not even a false slander might touch him. But when he proved unassailable to those who use every device against handsome youths, and no one, neither stranger nor citizen, not rich, not brave, not wise, nor distinguished for anything else, could persuade him to pay attention to him, certain men decided to disgrace his body through the tyrant and to force the one who would not yield.

And going, it seems, to him they said: 'You, a tyrant, able to inspire fear and hunting for pleasures, collect worthless little lads, but will not enjoy the most beautiful of all beneath the sun, and that though he is near?' Then, I suppose, they described his hair, his face, his hands, the rest, and how the youth is a challenge even to painters, since his beauty puts their art to the test.

With these words stirring him and inflaming him and making him a lover of one he had not seen, they persuade him to send that shameless embassy. The people had assembled, the envoys came forward, and there was hope that they had come to ask for something more reasonable, such as arms, grain, soldiers, or a reconciliation with certain exiles.

Even these would be outrageous, I think: that a man at war with freedom and with laws should negotiate with those who choose to live with them in order to obtain something; yet there would have been some reason in it. But what [did he say] through the envoys, O Earth and Sun and bitter Fate of my house? 'Since I delight in intercourse with youths, and a father among you is raising a son such as no one has in any city', and he said who and whose son, 'send me the young man, to suffer whatever I please.'

At this I covered my head and, struck to the soul, lay speechless on the knees of my friends, little different from a dead man, barely aware of the uproar which you raised, ashamed before the gods, ashamed before one another, ashamed before nature; and this when they added that, if you did not hand over his body, you would be at war, thinking to overcome your self-control by fear. But to you, it seems, it seemed more terrible than the expected hardships that such things should be given by you, and you grieved with the youths who were with him, and would most gladly have taken vengeance on behalf of those who had been outraged.

So you drove away the envoys, and he, having failed in what he demanded, at once attacked, having, it seems, his arms in hand even when he sent the envoys, so as to fall upon you unprepared. And at once the countryside was full of enemies, and the farmers streamed into the city bringing whatever of their goods they could; and to go out and fight was not possible, since the war and its horrors had fallen on us first, but shut in, we had to endure the evils of the siege. The present was grievous, the future fearful, no ally from anywhere, and the tyrant great. And among them was the shouting of the besiegers, among us the despondency of the shut-in.

14. Then I called none of my friends or kinsmen to counsel, but sitting by myself I talked with myself as a comrade with a comrade. 'Most unfortunate of fathers,' I said, 'you who acquired a son's beauty against yourself and your fatherland, you see the army surrounding the wall, the tyrant full of madness, and those ready to do anything for a master in love, and that the city cannot be saved as the evil advances. The cause of these things is your son and your son's beauty. And unless this either perishes or becomes the tyrant's, there is no release from the present troubles. Since, then, the outrage is unbearable, but death not so much, let him save the city together with his own chastity.'

This seemed best on the first day, this on the second, this on the third, and there was nothing that could be thought better than this. So I took up the sword and laid it down again, and taking it up again I threw it away, and [did] each of these many times, and each with tears. Then the [resolve] prevailed to give my son to the fatherland; and having struck my face many times and torn my hair and said to my own fate, 'Take your fill of my misfortunes,' by what I showed him I persuaded the tyrant no longer to seek what no longer existed. And the end of the boy has also become the end of the war.

After this I mourned, I buried [him], I clung to the tomb, I thought I ought to sit there. And indeed, seeing this fine fellow approaching, I thought he had come to do the same as the others and to console me. But he stood over me and, shouting savagely, said, 'Get up, you utter villain, and follow, to pay the penalty for these things,' which he has said now too, gentlemen. For he says that I have killed my son, and he asked whether this is not true and whether it is not terrible.

17. I admit that I have done this deed, but I cannot condemn myself of wickedness. Why? Because no one could show that the reason for what was done was wicked, and if the reason was not such, neither could the deed be thought wicked. How much this matters one could learn from many sources, but above all from the laws on damage, in which it makes no small difference whether [one acted] willingly or unwillingly. And in the laws on homicide one would find the same. And what? Have not generals often burned even their own ships and destroyed the crops, and been crowned for doing so? For they did it not to harm those who trusted them, but to harm those opposed to them. So when the intention is approved, the deed too is freed from blame.

So you too, do not pass over why it happened and speak only of what happened, but allow these men, my good sir, to cast their vote on the basis of everything. Now if you can show that I hated my own child, and was vexed when he was well and glad when he was sick, and turned away when he approached, and kept on beating and choking him, and was often shown cursing him to die before he became a man — if the prosecutor can charge any of these things, and not only charge them but also produce witnesses, kill me, cut me down, drown me in the sea, I will have nothing to say; but if I have been robbed of one whom I wanted to live, pity the man who has suffered loss. For how would it make sense to bring the work of the hand under examination, but to leap over what I intended in doing it?

I wish, gentlemen, that the tyrant during the siege had sent a herald to you to say that he had been defeated by your resolve not to give up the young man, 'but hand over to me his father, and [end] the war.' Then you would have seen clearly how I stood toward my own [son]. For I myself would have come forward and drafted the decree on the surrender, or rather, even before the decree, I would have run beneath the tyrant's swords, and I would have feared none of the horrors, since through them I was going to gain that one thing: that my son should live for me.

For why would I not have given myself up for him? Was he not reasonable? Not well-behaved? Not devoted to his father? Not such as to make his own ancestors more renowned, and, when he took up public affairs, to be second to none? For I will say no more. Did I not know that, both speaking in the assembly and serving as general, he, having sense together with beauty, would make you greater, and his father, even when dead, more illustrious?

I pass over the rest; but if someone asked you, the accusers, 'Why are you doing this?', you would say that you grieve for the youth. Then you grieve that he is dead, and I rejoice? Certainly I have discredited the killing by what [I did] after the death! Do you see me dressed in white, going to the baths, dining lavishly and singing at drinking parties? Do I not lie in ashes? Do I not resemble the dead? Do I not long for death? Was I then seeking these things, by whose happening I am ruined? And was I not even ashamed before the wild beasts' affection for their young?
22. What, then, was the reason for what was done? For must I answer this, when the judges, the bystanders, the whole city could not say it — children, women? But I must speak of what everyone knows.

23. A force had come against us, numerous and great, an army terrible and harsh: cavalry, hoplites, archers, slingers. The villages were being destroyed, the flocks seized, the trees cut down. The tyrant was master of the countryside, and he wanted the city too. And we saw the siege engines, and there was much shouting and abuse, general against taxiarch, taxiarch against soldiers, soldiers against their officers. Fears assailed us everywhere, alarming us just as the words did. The day was in turmoil, the nights sleepless, food not to the full. The end of the siege was not yet here, but it was seen in our reckonings.

Now if I had been able either to hit the tyrant with a missile from the battlements, or to go out to him and persuade him by words to depart, or to lead out a force and drive back the invader, I would have done wrong in not taking the field; but since none of these things could be done, and there was danger that the city would be taken, and there was only one remedy for the evil, I granted the city [him who] is no more.

If the occasion had demanded advice, I would have spoken; if a number of talents, I would have contributed; if a sortie, I would have gone out; if battle, I would have fought. Now then, since the occasion demanded my son, I did not shrink from this either. For one must pray that such necessities do not befall, but when they come, consider nothing higher than the city. The city received the one it reared, received the one it educated, [...]

Was it not this that everyone then prayed for in the temples and at the altars, old men, mothers, <sons>, daughters, and every family of priests: that the tyrant should cease from his rage, end the siege and lead away his force? What then? If one of the citizens gave you what you prayed to obtain, has he acted wickedly? Do you not hear that the Pythian [Apollo] has in this way helped many cities, with fathers obeying his oracles? And the children were sacrificed, and the horrors were halted. So it pleases even the gods that one body should depart for the sake of a city.

Over things unclear one must take refuge with them, but when what will benefit is clear, people must help themselves on the basis of what is evident. Our danger then was not about the boundaries of land, such that the loyal man need not do everything; the siege threatened the city with destruction. This, then, made the deed necessary.

28. Now this man asks me whether it is not terrible that the boy is dead, and I will ask him in return whether it is not terrible for the city to be razed. For that the tyrant, had he taken it, would have done this in his bitter grief, anyone would agree. Are you indignant, then, that this wall was not thrown down, and that of its inhabitants some were not killed and others led away — the former the men of military age and the old, the latter women and children? Are you indignant that fire did not consume the city, and do you prosecute the man through whom you have your private property, the public property, the temples, the laws, the arms, the money, the wives, the children, this very power to indict and to seat judges?

29. 'For the people,' he says, 'had decided to make war,' and rightly so, desiring glory and thinking it intolerable to furnish a tyrant's pleasures. But just as it was fitting for you to do this for me, so it was fitting for me to do what I have done for you. For the people must protect each of the citizens, and each of the citizens must care for the people more than for his own. You made war willingly for the sake of my house. From the same house, then, came to you the end of the war. Or ought I to have sat in luxury and said to myself, 'How fortunate the boy is! The whole city suffers and is worn down and perishes, so that nothing great or small may distress him'? Certainly not; but I said to myself what I had to, and counselled myself [to do that] than which I found nothing nobler.

For even if none of you said to his neighbour, 'But this man looks on like this while the city is being destroyed,' and did not blame the man who had drafted the decree about the war, nor himself for accepting such terms, still not all were so iron-hearted as not even to grieve in silence at what was happening, for one may think many things which one would not utter; and to me this, gentlemen, was more bitter than any childlessness. And if none of the terrible things seemed terrible, but the war was equally sweet to all, men, women, children, old men, free men, slaves, this very thing ought to have made me feel shame: that out of zeal for me they thought war sweeter than peace.

I repaid their eagerness with a fitting return. Or ought I to have sat and waited for someone to say to me, 'Fellow, it is in your power whether the city exists or not, and it is nobler to save it than to destroy it. Will you not rise up and do something bold, and show the city that you possess everything? Let the youth be shown dead to the tyrant, and we are saved'?

But not even if the wall were being shaken down would you ever have uttered these words to me. Yet I considered that I was hearing them from the circumstances themselves. So the fact that you had chosen war did not hinder my ambition; rather, the very act of rising up against so great a force out of consideration for the boy summoned the boy's father to the deed.

33. 'But the tyrant,' he says, 'would have gone away, giving up in the face of his labours, and it was not clear that he would prevail in any case.' Having taken the youth, gentlemen, he would have gone away; but without taking him, he would not. For his passion was great and violent, burning and pressing on him and not letting him even draw breath. What is the sign of this? He openly declared what he ought to have hidden, and that through an embassy. What no one has ever heard of anywhere: a youth's beauty was demanded before an assembly.

Did he then, failing to get him, feel shame and slink away and become better for not succeeding? Not in the least; but he was so out of his mind and so set on getting his beloved alone that he set out and came in person leading his force, thinking he must spend both lives and money and leave out nothing that led to this end, considering every hardship worth the prize.

And desiring so greatly, he also had preparations to give him confidence. He had great wealth in his palace, and that close at hand, many arms, strength, and military skill, and rivalry among his followers as to which of them would hunt down his beloved and bring him and put him into his hands.

To him [supplies] flowed in [in plenty] from many quarters, and at the same time he made use of what was ours, and many of the neighbouring peoples were present as his helpers, hating him but courting him out of fear; while for us everything grew worse each day, with our land lost, the gates shut, and our grain unable to hold out through a long siege. For no sooner had we given our reply than we were shut in, and famine was near.

37. What then would have drawn him off from the wall? Passion held him, his power urged him on as well, and time itself has delivered many besieged cities to many men. And in general, do you suppose that sitting down before a city for such a prize was burdensome to him? For what could be lighter for a lover than toils in which there are hopes of winning the beloved? Indeed, what pains them is not to suffer hardship for such ends, and the more frenzied know only two releases from their passion: to win or to die. And tyrants, the more they think it fitting for themselves to prevail everywhere, the more fiercely they contend.

Did you not see from above what the man did over the corpse, pouring himself over it and kissing it, gazing closely at each of the limbs, gladly bloodying himself with the youth's wounds? Did he not very nearly take the body and carry it home? Would anything, then, have persuaded this man to keep away from the boy while alive, when death scarcely did?

So it was wholly inevitable that the siege would end in capture, and that he would have not one youth any longer, but many of my son's age, many younger, many women and girls, some of whom he would have outraged himself, and others given to his bodyguards.

40. But let us suppose that, having pulled down the wall and taken the youth, he would have laid hands on none of the others, but would have departed as though they had willingly given [him] a friend and ally, rebuilding the fallen part of the wall and crowning the people. Yet even if he was going to spare all the others, and there was some god to give assurance of this, that after the capture it would suffice the victor to have the boy alone, not even so would it have been honourable for me to see him led away for such purposes, nor for him himself to live on such terms rather than die. For there is a life more bitter than death and a death sweeter than life, when death brings release from disgrace.

How many under tyranny have killed themselves so as no longer to live in lawlessness! How many have thrown themselves from heights when enemies pressed on them, so as not to be captured and enslaved! But my son was not going to be a slave, though that too is terrible, but to be forced no longer to be a male, to be counted among women, and to hear from the eunuchs: 'Yesterday we brought him a concubine, today he calls for you. See that you please him as much as you can, refusing nothing he asks.'

Spending his nights in such things, coming out from such things, learning instead of the education of home what can delight a tyrant in bed, what would he have done when his youthful bloom had passed? Would he have lived on there, cast aside? Or would he have returned here, bringing a fine freedom of speech from fine deeds? And what should I have done? Followed him and sung the wedding song? Or, staying here, prided myself on what came from him, that he had been preferred by the tyrant over his wife and had outdone every face? And from whom would he later have taken a wife, how would he have admonished children, in what festival would he have shared, what contests, what sacrifices? Would he not have lost even his name and been called after the outrage? A splendid life indeed, not even to be able to look his own slaves in the face.

Why then should he have had to live longing for death, when it was possible to escape such a life by death? Now he lives even though dead, for he is celebrated in song; but then he would have been dead while alive, voiceless from what he had suffered. I snatched the boy with the sword from a tyrant's outrage, since there was no other way. For indeed, if robbers were pursuing me and him and, on catching him, were going to outrage him in this way, I would have turned to the same remedy then too, before we were caught. For such are the lessons we have been taught by the laws and by democracy. So, even if the killing had brought no gain to the community, for the sake of him who was in peril of the utmost it was done of necessity. For if one had to die three times for the sake of chastity and so as not to lose it, would one not be buying the greater at the price of the lesser?

44. But to these points they have nothing to say; they make a charge of the fact that the deed was not done together with the people. 'And what prevented you,' he says, 'from telling them what you would do, and so, having persuaded them, proceeding to the deed?' First, gentlemen, because it would not have been the act of a man who saw the crisis that had overtaken us. For what would it have meant to move you from the towers to the assembly, and to order you to lay down your arms and sit listening to speeches, and to let the enemy shake down the wall, while leading you into a deliberation over a single person, in which the speeches would necessarily be long?

For many would have come forward to make accusations, some out of envy of me, some of the youth, while the wish to curry favour with the tyrant would have raised up others to oppose. And all would have had a plausible argument, that these things were neither lawful nor customary. For if not even now, after the deed is done, can they restrain themselves, but persuade those who have been saved to be indignant and to consider no longer being besieged a harm, who would have been the men giving an opinion on the matter while what the tyrant desired had not yet been destroyed?

But, if you like, let us grant that the moment then was one for assemblies and speeches, not arms, that the siege was no obstacle to these, and that no one would have opposed what they said, neither the others nor those who now accuse me. Even so, gentlemen, it was better that this be decided about my own [son] by me. For that would have given a handle to those wishing to [slander] you: that the father came forward to discharge his duty and, in a way, to lay a suppliant's branch on behalf of his son, so that no one would be angry with him on whose account the city was besieged, but the people abused his words to commit murder; and he said 'Kill him' in order to hear them shout 'We will save him', but they, unwilling to look at the speaker's intention, destroyed the young man on the strength of bare syllables.

These slanders, gentlemen, I removed. I did not allow a decree to stand that would bring you no fine reputation, but made the deed wholly the father's. About this, only a shameless man would say that I killed him out of hatred, whereas someone might perhaps have pinned this on the people, who were besieged on his account. Why, then, should I have both helped the people and harmed them, and mixed bad with good, when it was possible to give them the benefit unmixed with the worse? And which of the two would the people have done? Would they have allowed him to be killed? Then what wrong have they suffered, when what they would have approved has been done? Or would they have prevented it, thinking those who spoke against it were in their right minds? Then I did well not to hand them an occasion for a penalty against themselves.

48. But some people, gentlemen, are clever at hounding those who give up what is most precious for the city as though they were traitors. After a few words to them I will step down. What do you fear, my good sirs? That I will come forward and set my own contribution beside those that have won renown among you, and the present security beside the terrors of the siege, and ask the citizens for public maintenance, or a bronze statue, or a crown? But this fear of yours is idle. For I am not so insensible of my own misfortune as to keep appearing on the speaker's platform, abandoning the tomb, and to think of gifts, when living is painful to me.

Or are you afraid that, while I keep silent, it will come from those who admire what I did, and someone will come forward and propose on my behalf what I would never propose for myself? Take heart, my good sirs, take heart. For even if the people should give everything at once, they will not find anyone to accept it. May nothing ever again seem pleasant to me except death.

Are you not afraid, by the gods, that by doing such things you will seem to look to the tyrant and to serve his interests, and to have yourselves been the informers of the youth's ill-fated beauty, and now to be consoling him by making trouble for me? What more do you want to happen to you? I have lost that fine son of mine, I have lost him. No one will see him walking to school any more, or returning from it any more, or in the wrestling-schools any more, or in the gymnasia any more. I, the father of a fine son, the blessed one, lie low; I have fallen. I have my son's tomb in place of my son.

51. But this is not enough either for you or for the tyrant, and I must die at all costs? Very well. Then what need is there of an accusation? What need of a vote? What need of malicious prosecution? Come forward and propose that I be handed over to the lover of beautiful [boys]. I will not speak against it or utter a sound, and I will consider you not enemies but friends, giving me to a man at whose hands I must very quickly die. But do not kill me, gentlemen, as one who has been wicked and cruel and unjust towards his own son, and do not make the other fathers worse than me, if ever (may it not happen) a moment should come demanding the same greatness of spirit.

This one must pray to avert, but sensible people must expect it, since even among your present children I see some who promise such beauty as to stir the tyrant again. If, then, he makes an attack and sends embassies demanding such things and threatening, and you choose to fight and be besieged, must you not have men who, like me, will put an end to your troubles? And you would achieve this if you vote that the first man to have done it did no wrong.

And by the gods, fathers of handsome sons, if war comes again from a similar cause and the city's whole existence is at stake, let nothing appear an evil that could end this evil; but follow the example nobly, considering such an end an ornament both to yourselves and to the sons who depart, and do not fear the malicious prosecutors more than what the city and the defeated must suffer at the hands of the victors.

Will some citizen speak ill of you? But the whole city will admire you, or rather every democratic city. Will you not see your sons? But you will have the company of the words spoken about them, such as I myself now hear from the citizens who wish to be good and just.

55. What then? You, tyrant, lover in an evil way, you offender against nature, stop such revelling, fear the gods, dread reproach. You will not mock the soul of the youth who fell because of you, which now, as is fitting, dwells with those who rescued their own fatherlands by their own deaths.

56. My son, you know the care with which you were raised, with which you were educated, and how, whenever you were ill, I begged the gods to transfer the sickness to me. But when war surrounded the city because of your beauty, and the crisis did not permit you to live, you are gone, yet not without glory: you have left me in laments, but your own name in songs, having so bravely obeyed necessity, and having yourself so roused your hesitating father.

For when he perceived, gentlemen, that events were bringing us to this (I will say it, even if some disbelieve), when he saw me standing apart, pale and weeping, my hand trembling, he uttered that wonderful saying, worthy of every honour: 'Do not delay, father. End the siege quickly. And I shall have my chastity as a fine burial garment.'

58. Such, gentlemen, have we been towards you. Such has been our fortune, and such our resolve. If, having made this defence, I seem to you to deserve death, condemn me. But not even so shall I blame myself.
